# What the final model is

Before the ladder, the destination, because each rung only makes sense as
a step towards it.

The object being modelled is the single-trial voltage waveform at one
electrode, not a condition average. Write $y_{jnt}$ for the voltage of
subject $j$ on trial $n$ at time $t$, over an epoch from $-200$ to
$1000$ ms. The model is

$$
y_{jnt} \;=\; \alpha \;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{K} \beta_{jnk}\,\phi_k(t) \;+\; \epsilon_{jnt},
$$

where the $\phi_k$ are fixed Gaussian radial basis functions of time and
the weights decompose additively into a population term, systematic
effects of subject and stimulus properties, and random deviations:

$$
\beta_{jnk} \;=\; \underbrace{w_k}_{\text{population}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\textstyle\sum_{m} \gamma_{km}\,x_{jnm}}_{\text{covariates}}
\;+\; \underbrace{u_{jk}}_{\text{subject}}
\;+\; \underbrace{v_{nk}}_{\text{trial}} .
$$

Two features of this are worth stating explicitly, because they are the
whole reason for the approach.

Each covariate enters as a $K$-vector $\gamma_{\cdot m}$, not a scalar. A
unit change in numerical ratio, or a unit change in a subject's ANS
acuity, therefore changes the *shape* of the predicted waveform, and can
change it at one latency without changing it elsewhere. The model can be
asked which part of the waveform tracks task difficulty rather than being
told in advance.

Each grouping factor likewise gets a $K$-vector, so a subject or a trial
has its own random *function* of time, a whole waveform deviating from the
population waveform, not merely an amplitude offset.

The residual $\epsilon_{jn\cdot}$ is not iid. It is a draw from a
multivariate normal over the epoch, with a correlation structure estimated
from the data.

That is the target. Nothing below adds anything conceptually new to it.
The ladder exists because fitting it in one step would produce a model
that either fails or succeeds for reasons that cannot be identified, and
because each rung has a cheap frequentist counterpart already fitted in
`lme4` to be checked against.

## Why basis functions rather than a Gaussian process

A Gaussian process with a squared exponential kernel is the limit of this
model as $K \to \infty$ with iid weights, so the two are not different
model classes. The finite expansion is preferred here for three reasons,
all practical rather than theoretical.

The multilevel structure above is immediate for a finite expansion. A
subject-level random function is $K$ extra coefficients and a covariate
effect on waveform shape is $K$ extra coefficients, both handled by
machinery identical to random slopes in an ordinary mixed model. The
corresponding constructions for a GP are available but considerably less
transparent.

It is linear in its parameters given fixed centres and widths, so
everything known about linear regression applies unchanged, including the
interpretation of the priors below as penalties.

It can be explained to a general audience, which a GP cannot, and the
audience for this work is a psychology readership.

The cost of the choice is that the number and placement of the basis
functions become explicit modelling decisions rather than being absorbed
into a kernel. Section 3 is about how those decisions are handled.

# The basis

## Definition

The basis functions are Gaussian bumps in time,

$$
\phi_k(t) \;=\; \exp\!\left( -\frac{(t - \mu_k)^2}{2\,(c\,\ell_k)^2} \right),
\qquad k = 1, \dots, K,
$$

with centres $\mu_k$ and nominal widths $\ell_k$ supplied as data, and a
single global multiplier $c$ estimated. Collect them into the
$T \times K$ design matrix $B$ with $B_{tk} = \phi_k(t_t)$.

The centres are not estimated. Free centres are attractive in principle
and were considered, but at the values of $K$ used here the likelihood is
nearly flat under trading a shift in $\mu_k$ against a change in $w_k$, so
the centres are weakly identified and the posterior becomes multimodal.
Estimating one global width multiplier is the compromise. It removes the
need to guess the length scale, costs a single parameter that is usually
well identified, and leaves the geometry benign. Setting its prior scale
close to zero fixes the widths exactly, which recovers the previous
convention.

## Placement

Two densities, not one. A coarse set of $K_c = 8$ centres spanning the
whole epoch, and a denser, narrower set of $K_d = 8$ confined to
$0$ to $300$ ms, giving $K = 16$.

This is not arbitrary. It encodes the prior knowledge that the components
of interest, P1 at roughly 80 to 150 ms, N1 at 150 to 200 ms, and P2p at
200 to 250 ms, all sit inside that window, and that the epoch is
comparatively featureless outside it. It is also the placement the `lme4`
smoke tests arrived at empirically. With the coarse set alone, each basis
function about 170 ms wide, the population fit smoothed straight through
the early structure and flattened peak amplitude throughout. Adding the
dense tier fixed that.

The coarse block is ordered first. This matters, because the group-level
random functions below use only the first $K_c$ columns of $B$.

## What can and cannot be reported

Overlapping bumps are collinear. The condition number of $B$ at this
placement, on the 128 Hz grid, is about 350, and the consequence is heavy
cancellation between neighbouring weights. Individual $w_k$ are therefore
not separately interpretable and their marginals are unstable.

This does not damage prediction or inference about the fitted curve. It
does mean that every reported quantity must be a function of the fitted
curve, such as $f(240)$, the height of the fitted P2p peak, or the
difference between two fitted curves at a latency. It also means that the
basis functions are not expected to correspond one to one with ERP
components. Components are individuated by scalp topography and functional
dissociation, and the waveform at a single electrode is a superposition of
temporally overlapping sources. The components are properties of the
fitted curve, not of individual basis functions.

# The prior on the weights

## Why the obvious prior is wrong

The natural first choice is $w_k \sim \mathrm{N}(0, s^2)$ independently,
with $s$ fixed. In the earlier version of this model $s$ was set to 100
against data with a standard deviation of about 8 µV, which leaves the
weights effectively unpenalised. Combined with the collinearity above,
this is what produced fitted weights of order $10^2$ with large
cancellation between neighbours. The scale must at minimum be inferred.

But making $s$ a parameter is not sufficient, and the reason is worth
being precise about. An independent prior with a common scale is a ridge
penalty, $\lambda\|w\|^2$. It shrinks weights towards zero, which
penalises amplitude. It does not shrink them towards each other, which is
what penalises roughness. Under an independent prior the smoothness of the
fitted curve is controlled entirely by the widths $\ell_k$, which are
supplied as data. In other words, the amount of smoothing is asserted
rather than estimated.

## Ridge and curvature

Two components, both with estimated scales. Let $b(k)$ denote the density
block containing basis function $k$, and let $\Delta^2 w_k = w_k - 2w_{k-1} + w_{k-2}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
w_k &\sim \mathrm{N}\!\left(0,\ \tau^{\text{ridge}\,2}_{b(k)}\right), \\
\Delta^2 w_k &\sim \mathrm{N}\!\left(0,\ \tau^{\text{curv}\,2}_{b(k)}\right),
\qquad \text{for $k$ interior to its block.}
\end{aligned}
$$

Because the centres within a block lie on a grid, the weight sequence
indexed by $k$ is a sampled function of latency, and its second difference
approximates the second derivative of the fitted curve. Penalising
$\sum_k (\Delta^2 w_k)^2$ is therefore the discrete approximation to
penalising $\int f''(t)^2\,dt$, which is the standard spline roughness
penalty. The curvature component is a penalised spline penalty, written as
a prior, applied to a Gaussian RBF basis.

The two components are complementary rather than alternatives. Second
differences vanish when $w$ is linear in $k$, so the curvature prior
leaves a two-dimensional subspace per block unpenalised, and the ridge
component covers it. Without that, nothing prevents the pre-stimulus
baseline from drifting on an unpenalised linear trend in the weights. This
is the same construction as a cubic shrinkage spline, `bs = "cs"` in
`mgcv`, which is a cubic spline with a ridge component added to penalise
its own null space.

The scales are per block. The coarse and dense grids have spacings of
about 171 ms and 43 ms, so a second difference approximates $h^2 f''$ with
very different $h$, and a single scale would apply a different effective
amount of smoothing to the two blocks without that being anyone's
intention.

The curvature prior is applied *within* each block. The full basis is a
concatenation of two overlapping grids, so the required ordering does not
exist across the join.

The behavioural difference from a ridge prior alone is the point. A ridge
prior penalises a large P2p for being large. A curvature prior leaves large
excursions alone provided they are smooth, and penalises only rapid
change. The second is much closer to what is believed about the data.

## What this buys

Jointly, the two components mean that the effective complexity of the
fitted curve is controlled by four estimated scale parameters rather than
by $K$ and the spacing. This is the mechanism by which $K$ becomes close
to immaterial in a penalised spline, where the standard advice is to take
$k$ generously and check only that it was large enough. Adopting the
penalty adopts that property. The question of how many basis functions to
use is genuinely hard under an independent prior with a fixed scale, and
close to immaterial under this one.

There is a second benefit specific to this problem. The mean model and the
noise model both describe smooth low-frequency structure on the same
domain, so there is a real risk of the noise model absorbing signal. A
proper prior on the roughness of the mean model puts an explicit,
estimated bound on how rough the mean model can be, which limits how much
ongoing EEG it can absorb. Under a fixed, very wide independent prior,
nothing did.

## What is deliberately not used

A horseshoe or regularised horseshoe prior on the weights was considered
and rejected for this ladder, for three reasons.

It is not a smoothness prior. Neighbouring weights are independent under
it and a sparse set of heavy-tailed weights produces a spiky curve, which
works against what is wanted.

Its intended purpose here was basis selection, and selection is better
handled after fitting, by projection predictive selection, which evaluates
whether a subset of basis functions spans the fitted curve rather than
whether individual coefficients are nonzero. The latter question is not
answerable when the columns are as collinear as these. That work is
deliberately deferred and is not part of this ladder.

The geometry. The horseshoe funnel is difficult on its own, and it would
be added on top of a constrained AR parameterisation and several thousand
group-level coefficients.

# The noise model

## The general form

Let $y_n$ be the $T$-vector for curve $n$. The residual is a single draw
from a $T$-dimensional Gaussian,

$$
\epsilon_n \;\sim\; \mathrm{MVN}\!\left(0,\ \sigma^2 R\right),
\qquad R_{tt'} = \rho_{|t - t'|},
$$

with $R$ Toeplitz. The iid model is the special case
$\rho_h = \mathbb{1}[h=0]$, and it is not defensible here. The data were
band-pass filtered at 1 to 30 Hz and sampled at 1024 Hz, so nothing in the
record can change faster than 30 times a second while samples arrive a
thousand times a second. Empirically the residual autocorrelation under an
iid model is 0.77 at lag 1 and reaches $-0.46$ by lag 6.

Note what the noise model does and does not affect. Whatever is assumed
about $\epsilon$, the estimate of $w$ stays roughly unbiased. What changes
is its variance, since the noise model enters inference only through
$R^{-1}$. Under the iid model the standard error of the fitted waveform at
the P2p latency is understated by roughly 50%. The correlated noise model
is about calibration, not about fit.

## AR($p$), and why

$R$ is generated by a stationary autoregressive process of order $p$,

$$
\epsilon_t \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{p} \varphi_j\,\epsilon_{t-j} \;+\; a_t,
\qquad a_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathrm{N}(0, \sigma_a^2),
$$

with $\rho_h$ following from the $\varphi_j$ by the Yule-Walker recursion,
so the recursive form and the Toeplitz covariance matrix are two views of
one object rather than two models.

The choice of AR($p$) is not a choice of one kernel out of infinitely
many. It is a nested sequence whose spectral densities are rational
functions of $e^{-i\omega}$, and which can therefore approximate any
continuous spectral density bounded away from zero. That converts an
unstructured search over covariance functions into a one-dimensional
choice of order. A squared exponential kernel, by contrast, is a single
point with a fixed spectral shape and no dial to turn, it cannot produce
negative autocorrelations at all, and it is the limit of the mean model,
so using it in the residual would put two copies of the same model class
in competition.

AR(2) is adopted as the working default on physiological grounds. It is
the lowest order that can represent a rhythm: with complex roots the
autocorrelation function is a damped cosine, a discrete-time damped
harmonic oscillator. Fitted to a posterior electrode it recovers a
frequency near 11 Hz, which is the alpha rhythm, and that was not a target
of the fit. AR(1) cannot do this, since its autocorrelation is monotone
and never negative, and fitted here it degenerates to a random walk.

Order selection by likelihood is not well posed on a single trial and
should not be attempted. The criterion to use instead is stability: if the
posterior interval for the reported quantity is materially the same under
AR(2), AR(3) and AR(4), the order does not need resolving. If it changes,
that sensitivity is the finding.

## Parameterisation

Two things need care and one device handles both.

The AR coefficients must lie in the stationarity region, which for
general $p$ is not expressible as box constraints, and rejection sampling
on the constraint gives a discontinuous posterior and poor Hamiltonian
Monte Carlo behaviour. The model is therefore parameterised by the partial
autocorrelations $r_1, \dots, r_p$, each free in $(-1, 1)$, mapped to the
AR coefficients by the Levinson-Durbin recursion. The image of the open
cube $(-1,1)^p$ under this map is exactly the stationarity region, so
stationarity holds by construction with a smooth unconstrained geometry.

The same recursion gives the exact rather than conditional likelihood for
free. At time $t$ the best linear predictor of $\epsilon_t$ from its
predecessors uses the order-$\min(t-1, p)$ coefficients the recursion
produces along the way, with prediction variance
$\sigma^2 \prod_{i \le \min(t-1,p)} (1 - r_i^2)$. Accumulating these
one-step prediction errors gives the exact log-likelihood in $O(Tp)$, with
no $T \times T$ matrix formed and no Cholesky taken. This decomposition
has been verified against an explicit multivariate normal density and
agrees to machine precision, for $p = 0, 1, 2, 4$.

Note that $\sigma$ in this parameterisation is the *marginal* standard
deviation of $\epsilon$, not the innovation standard deviation. They
differ by $\prod_i (1 - r_i^2)^{1/2}$. The marginal scale is on the scale
of the observed data and is much easier to put a prior on.

Setting $p = 0$ recovers iid noise exactly, so one file fits both.

## Decimation

All models are fitted at 128 Hz, every eighth sample, giving $T = 154$
rather than 1229.

This is close to lossless. Because the whole record is band-limited at
30 Hz, not just the signal, the 1024 Hz samples are a deterministic
function of the 128 Hz samples, so the decimated data are a sufficient
statistic for anything in this model.

More importantly it is necessary rather than merely permitted. At 1024 Hz
a low-order AR likelihood degenerates: the innovation standard deviation
collapses towards zero, the autoregressive roots crowd onto the unit
circle, and the posterior geometry becomes badly conditioned. See the
technical appendix for why this is a necessary consequence of
band-limiting rather than bad luck, and for the one implementation detail
that matters, which is that decimation requires an anti-alias filter and
plain subsampling is not decimation.

# The ladder

Four models. Each adds one thing.

## B0. One subject, one trial

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_t &\sim \mathrm{N}\!\left(\mu_t,\ \cdot\right), &&
  \epsilon = y - \mu \sim \mathrm{MVN}(0, \sigma^2 R(r)), \\
\mu_t &= \alpha + \sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k\,\phi_k(t).
\end{aligned}
$$

Priors:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha &\sim \mathrm{N}(0, 10^2), \\
w_k &\sim \mathrm{N}(0, \tau^{\text{ridge}\,2}_{b(k)}), &
\Delta^2 w_k &\sim \mathrm{N}(0, \tau^{\text{curv}\,2}_{b(k)}), \\
\tau^{\text{ridge}}_b &\sim \mathrm{N}^{+}(0, 10^2), &
\tau^{\text{curv}}_b &\sim \mathrm{N}^{+}(0, 10^2), \\
c &\sim \mathrm{LogNormal}(0, 0.15^2), &
\sigma &\sim \mathrm{N}^{+}(0, 10^2), \\
r_i &\sim \mathrm{U}(-1, 1).
\end{aligned}
$$

Nothing is multilevel. The purpose is to establish that the basis, the
decimation, the prior on the weights and the noise model all behave on a
single waveform, where there are few enough moving parts that a failure
can be attributed. Fit it at $p = 0$, $p = 2$ and $p = 4$ and look at
whether the reported amplitude at 240 ms is stable across them.

What to check. The fitted curve should track the waveform without chasing
it, and the residual should absorb the fast wiggle. The weights should no
longer be of order $10^2$. The implied AR(2) frequency should be
recognisable. The posterior for $c$ should be inspected to see whether the
nominal widths were about right.

File: `stan/rbf_b0_single_trial.stan`, driver `R/fit_b0.R`.

## B1. Subject variability

Curves are subject averages, one per subject, $j = 1, \dots, J$. Let
$B_r$ denote the first $K_c$ columns of $B$.

$$
\mu_{jt} \;=\; \alpha \;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k\,\phi_k(t)
\;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{K_c} u_{jk}\,\phi_k(t),
\qquad u_{jk} \sim \mathrm{N}\!\left(0, \tau^{\text{subj}\,2}_k\right),
$$

with $\tau^{\text{subj}}_k \sim \mathrm{N}^{+}(0, 10^2)$ and the
population priors as in B0. The residual is AR($p$) within subject.

Three points on the specification. Each basis function gets its own scale
with no covariance between basis dimensions, matching the uncorrelated
random slopes used in the `lme4` counterpart, and much likelier to behave
than a full $K_c \times K_c$ covariance matrix. The subject deviations use
only the coarse block, which is where the smoothness control at the group
levels comes from, a point returned to at B2. And averaging over roughly
180 trials divides the residual variance by about 180 while leaving the
autocorrelation structure alone, so $\sigma$ is much smaller here than
elsewhere in the ladder and its prior scale must reflect that.

This is the direct counterpart of `lme4` model M0, which fitted in 240
seconds and converged cleanly on all 47 subjects. The comparison to make
is whether the population curve agrees. Where it does not, the difference
should be explicable as shrinkage.

The specific gain over the `lme4` fit is visible in
$\tau^{\text{subj}}_k$. In `lme4`, a weakly identified variance component
produced a degenerate Hessian and an outright optimiser failure, since
REML has no way to shrink such a component gracefully towards zero. Here
it shrinks smoothly and the posterior says so. That failure mode, hit
repeatedly across the three smoke tests, is the reason for moving to Stan.

## B2. Trial variability

One subject, every trial, nothing averaged. Curves are trials,
$n = 1, \dots, N$.

$$
\mu_{nt} \;=\; \alpha \;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k\,\phi_k(t)
\;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{K_c} v_{nk}\,\phi_k(t),
\qquad v_{nk} \sim \mathrm{N}\!\left(0, \tau^{\text{trial}\,2}_k\right),
$$

with AR($p$) residual within trial.

The restriction of the trial deviations to the coarse block is the
substantive decision here, and it is carried over from the `lme4` pass
rather than rediscovered. Giving trials all 16 basis functions produced
visible single-trial overfitting, with individual trial fits tracking what
looked like noise, worst in the eight dense narrow functions, which are
exactly the ones capable of representing that kind of fine structure.
Restricting to the coarse eight removed that capacity directly rather than
shrinking flexibility everywhere by an arbitrary amount.

This is also why a curvature prior is not applied at the group levels. The
coarse basis has a spacing of 171 ms and cannot produce a rough curve, so
the restriction already does the work. The construction for a curvature
prior on the random effects is given in the technical appendix should it
turn out to be needed.

Leave-one-trial-out cross-validation becomes available at this rung, and
is the right unit. The Stan model returns one log-likelihood value per
curve rather than per timepoint. Leaving out a single timepoint from an
autocorrelated series is nearly free and says almost nothing, whereas
trials are exchangeable within subject in a way that neighbouring
timepoints are not.

Counterpart: `lme4` model M1, 745 seconds.

## B3. Subjects and trials together

Both grouping factors, crossed.

$$
\mu_{nt} \;=\; \alpha
\;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k\,\phi_k(t)
\;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{K_c} u_{s(n)k}\,\phi_k(t)
\;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{K_c} v_{nk}\,\phi_k(t),
$$

where $s(n)$ is the subject of curve $n$, and the residual is AR($p$)
within curve. Priors as in B1 and B2 combined.

This is the target structure of the ladder and by a wide margin the
expensive one. The trial level alone carries $K_c \times N$ coefficients.
At 47 subjects and 10 trials each that is about 3,800, and at the full
trial count it would be on the order of $10^5$.

Two consequences follow, and they are not optional.

Cut trials, not subjects. The `lme4` pass established this by getting it
wrong twice. Reducing to 15 subjects reproduced the degenerate Hessian,
because 15 groups cannot support eight variance components, and cutting
the subject basis to two functions produced numerically unstable nonsense
because with two centres the width convention forces the width to the
whole epoch and the two functions become nearly collinear. The number of
trial groups is subjects times trials per subject and stays large however
few trials per subject are kept, so trial count is the safe dimension.

Do not go straight to HMC. Run Pathfinder, then Laplace, then sampling.
The mean model is linear in $w$, so conditional on the noise and scale
parameters the posterior is close to Gaussian and the approximations
should do well, with the departures from normality concentrated in
$\sigma$, $r$ and the $\tau$. That is a hypothesis to check by comparison
against HMC on the fitted curve, not an assumption, and checking it is
what makes fast iteration possible later.

For context, the `lme4` counterpart M2 took 71 minutes at 20 trials per
subject and 1229 timepoints. At 154 timepoints the per-gradient cost is
eight times lower, but HMC needs many gradient evaluations, so expect
hours.

There is a known open question at this rung, unresolved and carried over.
In the `lme4` fit, trial-level spread was largest at the two epoch edges,
which looks more like a basis boundary artefact than a finding about
neural variability, since the outermost weights are the least constrained
by data. Whether the curvature prior reduces it is one of the things to
check. If it does not, the remedy is to extend the coarse centres beyond
the epoch rather than to add more inside it.

# What comes after the ladder

Explicitly out of scope here, and listed so that it is clear what the
ladder is a foundation for rather than a substitute for.

Stimulus and subject covariates, the $\gamma_{km}$ of section 1. This is
B4 and it is the first rung that answers a scientific question rather than
checking machinery. It is structurally identical to the group-level terms
already present, so it should be cheap to add once B3 runs.

Multiple electrodes. Electrodes are not exchangeable the way subjects and
trials are, since they sit at fixed points with a real geometry, and an
unstructured random intercept per electrode would discard that. Handling
it properly means a smooth model over scalp coordinates. One electrode at
a time until then.

Children as well as adults, and population comparisons.

Projection predictive selection of the basis, for interpretability rather
than for fit.

Analytic marginalisation of the trial-level coefficients, which would
remove on the order of $10^5$ parameters and the funnel geometry they
bring. See the appendix. This is an efficiency measure to be taken only
once B3 is understood, not before.
